headline: China's AI Trade Has Moved On From Consumer Internet to Chips
lede: KWEB, the $6.9 billion KraneShares ETF that defined China internet investing for a decade, is full of companies — Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu — that were the future once and are now mature platforms still nursing the scars of Beijing's 2021 regulatory crackdown. The companies actually building China's AI infrastructure — domestic chip designers, fab-equipment makers, and semiconductor material suppliers that China needs because it can no longer freely import Nvidia GPUs — list on a different exchange, track a different index, and are captured by a different ETF. That ETF is KSTR, and the performance gap between the two is impossible to ignore.
body:
**KWEB** — the KraneShares CSI China Internet ETF — was the canonical single-ticket for China internet exposure when Alibaba (BABA), Tencent (0700.HK), and Baidu (BIDU) felt like the future of the world's second-largest economy. That future arrived, then got badly complicated. Beijing's 2021 regulatory crackdown on its consumer internet sector — record antitrust fines, gaming restrictions, a cancelled Ant Group IPO, Didi forced off app stores days after its US listing — sent KWEB down roughly 58% from its February 2021 peak. By mid-2026 the five-year return stands at negative 49%. The fund holds roughly $6.9 billion in assets, which testifies more to inertia than conviction.

The “late 2010s-coded” label stings because it is accurate. KWEB's index — restricted by design to companies listed on Hong Kong, NASDAQ, or NYSE — captures China's consumer internet era: e-commerce, food delivery via Meituan (3690.HK), gaming, *super-apps*. These are platforms that monetize consumer attention and commerce. They are, in the language of the current moment, *AI users* — firms deploying large language models as product features, not companies building the hardware stack that makes AI possible.

KSTR — the KraneShares SSE STAR Market 50 Index ETF — tracks a different China entirely. The *SSE STAR Market* is Shanghai's answer to NASDAQ: a domestic listing venue for high-growth technology companies, launched in 2019, that cannot or will not list overseas. Its 50 largest constituents are overwhelmingly hardware. At roughly 14% of the fund, **Cambricon Technologies** (688256.SS) is the dominant position: the company designs *AI accelerator chips* for cloud training and edge inference, and its revenue grew more than 4,000% in the first half of 2025 as Chinese AI labs shifted from sanctioned Nvidia (NVDA) GPUs to domestic alternatives. Cambricon has confirmed day-zero software compatibility with DeepSeek's latest model. Hygon Information Technology (688041.SS), at roughly 11% of the fund, began as a joint venture with Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) to produce x86-compatible server CPUs; it has since expanded into GPU design and, after merging with state-owned HPC provider Sugon, now builds a full compute platform. Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment (688012.SS) — known as AMEC — makes the plasma etch and *CVD* tools that semiconductor fabs need, precisely the category targeted by US export controls on foreign suppliers.

The access problem is structural. KWEB's index methodology explicitly excludes *A-shares* — renminbi-denominated shares listed on mainland Chinese exchanges; it can only hold companies listed in Hong Kong or on US exchanges as *ADRs*. The most strategically consequential Chinese AI companies list domestically on the STAR Market because US IPOs became politically fraught after Didi's 2021 delisting disaster, and because domestic listing helps them retain state research contracts. KSTR, sub-advised by ICBC-UBS Asset Management, is the only US-listed ETF tracking the STAR 50 index. There is zero holdings overlap between the two funds. The sanctioned-equipment angle reinforces the distinction: AMEC's domestic etch tools fill the gap left by Applied Materials (AMAT) and Lam Research (LRCX) under US export controls, and that substitution trade lives entirely inside KSTR, not KWEB.

The performance gap has been stark. KSTR returned roughly 80% in the twelve months to May 2026; KWEB lost approximately 10% over the same period. The caveats are real: KSTR holds only about $116 million in assets against KWEB's $6.9 billion, making it prone to wider bid-ask spreads and steeper drawdowns, and its top two holdings account for roughly a quarter of the fund. Geopolitical risks also run in opposite directions — KSTR's chip companies sit on US export-control lists, constraining their access to leading-edge fabrication tools, while KWEB's ADR-listed holdings carry residual delisting risk under SEC audit-compliance rules. Neither is a safe harbour. But for an investor whose thesis is specifically that China's forced semiconductor self-sufficiency will generate extraordinary returns for the companies building that stack, KSTR is the precise instrument; KWEB is a category error.

concepts.definition: The Science and Technology Innovation Board (科创板), launched by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in July 2019 as China's domestic answer to NASDAQ. It allows high-growth technology companies — including those that are pre-profit or face barriers to overseas listing — to raise capital domestically. Its 50 largest constituents by market cap form the STAR 50 Index, which KSTR tracks.

A share of a company listed on the Shanghai or Shenzhen stock exchanges, denominated in Chinese renminbi and historically restricted to domestic investors. Foreign investors can access A-shares through specific programmes (QFII licences or the Hong Kong–Mainland Stock Connect), but many STAR Market companies are not covered by Connect, making US-listed ETFs like KSTR one of the few indirect routes for offshore investors.

American Depositary Receipt: a US-listed certificate, issued by a US bank, that represents ownership in shares of a foreign company. Chinese companies like Alibaba and Baidu trade as ADRs on NYSE and NASDAQ. ADRs carry an additional layer of geopolitical risk: the SEC's audit-inspection requirements have periodically threatened mass delistings of Chinese ADRs, most acutely during 2021–2022.

A specialised semiconductor designed to perform the matrix-multiplication operations at the heart of AI training and inference far more efficiently than a general-purpose CPU. Nvidia's H100 is the best-known example; Cambricon's Siyuan series is China's leading domestic equivalent, designed to train and run large language models without relying on sanctioned foreign silicon.

Chemical vapour deposition: a manufacturing process used in semiconductor fabrication to deposit ultra-thin films of material onto a silicon wafer. Along with plasma etching, CVD equipment is a critical step in building advanced chips, and it is among the categories covered by US and allied export controls targeting China's chip industry — making domestic suppliers like AMEC strategically important.

A mobile application that bundles a wide range of services — messaging, payments, ride-hailing, food delivery, social media — into a single platform. WeChat (Tencent) and Alipay (Ant Group) are the canonical examples. The super-app model dominated China's consumer internet era and remains the primary revenue engine for KWEB's largest holdings.

A shorthand for companies that deploy AI as a feature in existing products — e.g., Alibaba adding LLMs to its e-commerce search — as opposed to companies that manufacture the hardware or develop the foundational infrastructure that makes AI computation possible. The distinction matters for investors because in a supply-constrained environment, the hardware layer (chips, fab equipment) typically captures more pricing power than the application layer.

fact_check: Citrini's tweet describes KSTR as holding 'all the exciting Chinese AI companies,' which overstates the case. KSTR tracks the STAR 50 index — the 50 largest companies on Shanghai's innovation board — and its portfolio is dominated by semiconductor hardware: chip designers, fab-equipment makers, and memory-interface suppliers. Many of the most prominent Chinese AI companies by public profile (ByteDance, Moonshot AI, Zhipu AI, Manus AI) are either private or not STAR 50 constituents, and are therefore absent from KSTR. The fund is the best available US-listed vehicle for China's AI hardware buildout; it is not a comprehensive basket of Chinese AI.
